text.p: Pakistani President Farooq Leghari issued an anti-corruption decree on Monday under which convicted politicians can be disqualified for elections scheduled to take place on February 3.

The law was aimed at cracking down on corruption by politicians and bureaucrats but excluded the president and members of judiciary and armed forces from its purview, the caretaker government's Law, Justice and Parliamentary Affairs Minister, Fakhruddin Ebrahim, told a news conference.
Nonetheless, he said military officers working in state-run corporations could be tried under the new ordinance.
The law is being introduced 13 days after Leghari dissolved the lower house of parliament and sacked prime minister Benazir Bhutto on disputed charges of corruption and misrule.

Offences triable under the decree could result in up to seven years' prison and five-years disqualification for public representatives to contest elections and termination of service for government officials, Ebrahim said. They are non-bailable.
Politicians would not be barred from contesting elections merely if there were cases pending against them, he said.
But the decree offers an amnesty from jail to all those in public office who declare their corrupt practices and return illegally earned properties voluntarily within 10 days, Ebrahim said.
"(Those making such declarations) will of course stand disqualified for five years if he is holder of a public office and if a bureaucrat he will cease to hold his post," Ebrahim said.

He said the law would be made applicable from December 31, 1985, when late military ruler General Mohammad Zia-ul-Haq lifted martial law after 8-1/2 years. It would cover assets acquired through corrupt means, even if held under anonymous names or by dependents.
"The law applies to public representatives and the federal and provincial officers...in corporations, banks, financial institutions, firms, concerns, undertakings...," he said.
"It also extends to officers in the armed forces of equivalent status working in such organisations," he added.

He said the law excluded the president and the governors of the four provinces who have constitutional protection from criminal proceedings while in office. It would also not apply to members of the judiciary on similar grounds.

Bhutto's government and the main opposition Pakistan Muslim League had placed separate anti-corruption bills in front of the National Assembly (lower house) before Leghari dissolved the Assembly on November 5.

Bhutto says the fear of the anti-corruption law brought by her government, which was also applicable to the president, was one of the factors that prompted Leghari to order her sacking, which she has challenged before the Supreme Court.

Ebrahim said a chief accountability commissioner would be appointed by the president under the new decree to investigate a case within a month after it was referred. If a prima facie case were established, the commissioner would refer the case to a provincial high court for trial, which must be completed within 60 days.
